title: One-nighters in the South, Earle Warren on the train and Basie's bridges
summary: One-nighters through the South were rough. Light-skinned Earle Warren was told to leave the white coach, and later got food for the band in segregated towns. Basie would get off the bus to walk across rickety bridges.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That's funny. Well, so of course, they were always one-nighters, weren't they?
Yeah.
Not very often with theaters. And that's very rough.
It is rough.
And especially when they're all through the South.
Yeah.
Any of the guys too hot tempered, you know?
No, they were, everybody was alright. I remember one time we got on the train and you know, Earle Warren ?
Yeah.
He's just as white as you can get them.
Yeah, white folks, they call them.
Yeah. And so Earle was sitting there
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

in the coach with us and the conductor came and he said, "look here you, you got to get out of here". Earle said, "I don't know why". And he said, "we don't have no mixed". Earle said, "well I'm not white". He said, "you ain't fooling us. You go on up there in the next car". And then when Earle got ready to get off he said, " see there you had me up in that car and I'm going".
How funny.
We had Earle go into different places and get us food, you know.
Yeah.
When we were down South. That was just the way it was.
Yeah. Well, and Basie would ride right there with everybody else?

Yeah, he'd ride right with everybody else. And when we'd get down South we'd have to go over some ricketty bridges and Basie would say, 'stop the bus'. He'd get off and walk across the bridge. He was scared the bus was too big for them little old bridges you know. Sometimes a whole lot of them would get out and walk across.
